map.title: How GroupLab works
map.lead: Click any part for a technical summary, then open its full explanation. Or follow one target through the {fig:stages} stages of the pipeline's specification, from the file to the pooled group.
map.footnote: Arrows of control run downward: an app calls the Core, the Core calls the imaging interface, and the Core never touches OpenCV itself; the apps use OpenCV behind that interface and to read and write image files. The build-time checks and the online parts never run on your device.

parts.name: Desktop app
summary: An Avalonia shell around the Core. It prints sheets, runs the printer check, reads scans and photographs, and draws every result; the figures themselves all come from GroupLab.Core. Its imaging backend is OpenCvSharp with OpenCvSharp's own native runtime packages.

numbers.label: to analyze a 300 dpi Letter scan on a desktop, naming the sheet included

parts.name: Android app
summary: The same Core on the phone, with OpenCV built from source for arm64. The camera screen analyzes a {fig:android-stream} stream live (CameraX's default is {fig:camerax-default}, where a QR module is about one pixel), gives one instruction at a time, and in Guided mode fires after {fig:ready-frames} ready frames in a row. Every picture is then checked and scored. Its screens are one shared project, mobile/GroupLab.Mobile, a plain .NET library the iPhone and iPad build links too, and only the camera, printing, sharing and updating are Android's own.

parts.name: iPhone and iPad
summary: Planned the same way: an Avalonia shell around the same Core, with OpenCV built as a static iOS framework and builds from GitHub's macOS runners to TestFlight.

parts.name: Command line
summary: The engine with no windows. Its measurements are made by named commands, such as grouplab holes synthetic for the detector's scores or grouplab identify sweep for the QR reading, and the Phase 0 measurement record and the QR sweep are rerun by those commands in CI on Windows, Linux and macOS.

parts.name: Target format
summary: Every sheet is one GLTD definition: bulls, rings, markers, codes and the zones that can never hold a shot. A binary frame, GLTD-B, is printed in the QR codes: the whole definition, a CRC-32 over it and a tile index, so a sheet names its own definition. A wrong name must never happen, because it would scale every measurement by a wrong number; an unnamed sheet only costs one choice from a list.

numbers.label: Phase 0 images named from their codes, on Windows, Linux and macOS alike
wrong names on any platform, the number that must stay at zero

read.label: Designing a target GroupLab can read

parts.name: Renderer
summary: Draws the definition twice: as the PDF you print, and as the expected image, resampled through the registration so the printed artwork lies on the photo pixel for pixel. Paper level is estimated locally (the {fig:paper-pct} percentile of paper pixels in {fig:paper-block-words} blocks, smoothed), never as one global value.

numbers.label: blocks for the local paper level
most each bull cell may shift to align by phase correlation

parts.name: Registration
summary: Maps image pixels to page coordinates from the marker corners. Scans get a homography, never less than affine because scanners shear by {fig:scanner-shear}. Photographs add two radial lens terms fitted by Levenberg-Marquardt. Curled or waved paper is followed by a thin-plate spline through every corner.

numbers.label: corners from the {fig:markers-ltr} markers on GL-CF25-LTR, for an {fig:unknowns}-parameter homography
worst bull on {fig:printed-sheets} printed sheets, against a {fig:reg-gate} gate
inches, median worst bull on {fig:lens-photos} photos, without and with the lens fit

parts.name: Hole detection
summary: Subtracts the expected image from the photo, as a fraction of the local paper-to-ink range, so printed artwork cancels and holes remain. Then morphology sized in inches, not pixels: open with a radius of {fig:open-r}, threshold at {fig:threshold}, close with a radius of {fig:close-r}, fill, convex hull. The smallest hole allowed follows the stated caliber, one hole or two is judged against the sheet's own marks, and nothing is refused silently.

of held-out synthetic holes found within {fig:found-within}, one per bull; synthetic holes are easier than real ones, so this is an upper bound
median center error on those holes

parts.name: Statistics
summary: Mean radius, CEP 50 and 90, extreme spread and the rest, each with an interval. Mean radius is estimated as sigma times the square root of pi over two, not a plain average. Every figure the R package shotGroups also computes is checked against its output on every build. The simulation behind Shots Needed to Zero lives here too.

numbers.label: values compared with R shotGroups, none pending
Monte Carlo table cells within tolerance

parts.name: Ballistics
summary: Turns a group into what it means at distance: drop and wind for the load, a group carried to another distance, and the chance of a hit on a given target.

layers.label: Imaging
layers.note: the Core's only door to OpenCV

parts.name: OpenCV, behind one interface
summary: The Core never calls OpenCV. It asks an interface for seven things: find markers, fit a homography, warp, open or close, list filled blobs with hulls, phase-correlate, and read QR codes. Four floating-point steps, the warp among them, were moved into GroupLab's own managed code, so every platform prints the same figures.

numbers.label: operations the Core asks of OpenCV
OpenCV modules in the Android build
steps rewritten in managed code so every platform prints the same figures

parts.name: Reference checks
summary: Never shipped. The statistics are checked against R's shotGroups, the geometry and the QR format against independent Python code, and the ballistics against two other solvers, every time GroupLab is built. Neither R nor Python runs in the build: the tests read the outputs those programs wrote once and committed.
The original hole survey was also a Python and OpenCV harness, kept so each of its numbers can be reproduced.

parts.name: grouplab.org
summary: One script builds the whole site from plain files: the features list, the tour and the research articles. It refuses to build a figure that has no dark version, and it runs each article's figure script so the charts come from the data.

parts.name: Server workers
summary: Small PHP receivers put what arrives into quarantine, and small timed jobs under systemd limits take it from there. A sent target is rebuilt from its pixels (so nothing hidden in the file survives), is copied to a private archive, and is deleted from the server.

parts.name: Builds and updates
summary: Every change is built and tested on Windows, Linux and macOS. Every tested change to what ships becomes a nightly build with installers, and the app only accepts updates signed with the project's key.

steps.name: Print
steps.text: The renderer draws the sheet from its GLTD definition, with AprilTag markers where the cell lines cross and the definition in its QR codes. A one-time printer check measures the printer's scale, so photographs of its sheets are corrected to real inches.

steps.name: Shoot
steps.text: Nothing runs. The paper stretches ahead of the bullet and closes behind it, so a hole is narrower than the bullet: {fig:ratio-about} of caliber for .264 and .308 in the survey.

steps.text: A scan or a photo is decoded into one image, and the sheet is named from its QR codes.

stages.text: print scale reported per axis, never silently corrected

opencv.description: The seven OpenCV operations GroupLab uses, the defaults it had to change, and the parts that are GroupLab's own code.
opencv.title: How GroupLab uses OpenCV
opencv.lead: OpenCV is a widely used open-source computer vision library. GroupLab uses a small, deliberate slice of it: seven operations, reached through one interface, and one of the seven, the warp, has since become GroupLab's own code. OpenCV finds things in pixels. Deciding what a hole is, fitting the paper, and every number you are shown is GroupLab's own code.

stats.caption: the OpenCV release on every platform, built for each
operations the Core may ask for, and no others
OpenCV modules compiled into the Android build
floating-point steps moved into GroupLab's own code

sections.heading: Four layers between the Core and the pixels
sections.intro: GroupLab.Core has no reference to OpenCV at all. It talks to an interface, IImagingBackend, and each app plugs in an implementation. That keeps the measuring code identical on every device, lets tests swap the backend, and means a future library change touches one file rather than the engine.

cards.title: GroupLab.Core
cards.text: Registration, render-and-difference, classification, assignment, statistics. Asks for pixel work only through the interface below.

cards.title: IImagingBackend
cards.text: DetectMarkers · FindHomography · WarpPerspective · Morphology · FilledBlobs · PhaseCorrelate · ReadCodes

cards.title: OpenCvSharp
cards.text: A thin C# layer over OpenCV's C++ API, under the Apache-2.0 license. The managed half is one package; the native half must come from the same release.

cards.title: Desktop and command line
cards.text: OpenCvSharp's published native runtimes at {fig:opencv-version}, for Windows, Linux x64 and macOS, Intel and Apple silicon.

cards.title: Android
cards.text: Nobody publishes this, so GroupLab builds it: OpenCV and opencv_contrib {fig:opencv-version} compiled with the Android NDK for arm64-v8a, API {fig:android-api}, static C++ runtime, linked into one libOpenCvSharpExtern.so. The only community build carried {fig:community-modules} modules; GroupLab needs {fig:android-modules}.

items: **The Android modules.** core, imgproc, imgcodecs, **calib3d** for the homography, features2d, flann, **objdetect** for the QR decoder, dnn, **aruco** for the markers and **wechat_qrcode** for the QR finder. dnn is compiled in only because the WeChat finder needs it; no neural network is ever loaded, and no model file ships with GroupLab.

sections.heading: Everything GroupLab asks of OpenCV

head: Operation
OpenCV
Stage
What GroupLab sets, and why
rows: OpenCV's own corner refinement left off and every corner refined to a fraction of a pixel in GroupLab's code; threshold window and minimum perimeter sized from the expected marker; corner order turned back 180 degrees; a side-ratio gate of {fig:side-ratio} applied after decoding.
Threshold in page units. Correspondences sorted by marker identifier first, because RANSAC samples by list position. Final refinement done in managed code.
none now: GroupLab's own resampler, in place of imgproc warpPerspective

Resampling an image through a transform, as OpenCV's warpPerspective does with linear interpolation. Through the interface it builds only the synthetic scans of the registration check, and it runs in managed code so they match on every platform. The expected image in S5 has a resampler of its own.
Radii given in inches and converted with the measured scale: open radius {fig:open-r}, close radius {fig:close-r}.
Each outline filled, then each blob with its pixel count, box and convex hull, the hull being what is measured.
Aligns each bull cell of the expected image to the photo, up to {fig:cell-shift}, so a small registration error does not leave slivers.

WeChat finds, the plain decoder reads the bytes. Tried at full, double, half and quarter size, with the corners of the page tried when the whole finds nothing; then each code is cut out where the markers put it and read enlarged {fig:crop-scales} times.

sections.heading: How one AprilTag becomes four precise corners
sections.intro: Today's GroupLab Letter sheet, GL-CF25-LTR, carries {fig:markers-ltr} markers: {fig:markers-lattice} where the cell lines of its 5 by 5 grid cross, and {fig:markers-sighters} below its row of three sighter bulls. Each is an AprilTag from the 36h11 family: an 8 by 8 grid of {fig:marker-module} squares, a black border around {fig:tag-bits} data bits. What GroupLab needs from them is not their identity so much as their corners, measured to a fraction of a pixel.

items.caption: **1. The photo.** Gray, soft, turned and at an angle.
**2. Adaptive threshold.** Black or white against the local average, so shadows do not matter. Window sized for the marker.
**3. A quad.** Outlines become four-sided shapes. Too small, or sides more than 2 to 1, and it is refused.
**4. Straightened and sampled.** The perspective is removed and each data cell is read at its center.
**5. Decoded.** Matched against every code of the family, so a few misread bits are corrected and one marker is never taken for another.
**6. Corners refined.** Edges fitted through the gray pixels place each corner to a fraction of a pixel, in GroupLab's own code.

items: Each marker's {fig:tag-bits} data bits are matched against the family's {fig:tag-codes} codes, any two of which differ in at least {fig:tag-distance} bits. The family could correct up to {fig:correct-cap} misread bits; GroupLab corrects at most {fig:correct-used} and refuses the rest.

cards.title: Why 36h11
cards.text: {fig:tag-codes} identifiers, a minimum distance of {fig:tag-distance} bits between any two, and the only strong family that both OpenCV and the BSD-licensed AprilTag reference code can read. The first draft chose ArUco 6x6. Checking the claims it rested on reversed it: the AprilTag library cannot read any ArUco dictionary, and OpenCV draws 36h11 in the same 8 by 8 footprint. On the real scans both families scored zero false markers.

cards.title: Why 0.5 mm squares
cards.text: Detection needs about {fig:px-per-module} a square. The printer is the real limit: under about {fig:printer-dots} a square, ink spread shifts the edges, and the corner is the measurement. 0.5 mm gives {fig:px-600} a square on a 600 dpi scan and {fig:px-12mp} on a 12 MP photo.

cards.title: Why so many
cards.text: Four markers are enough for a flat scan. The {fig:markers-ltr} on GL-CF25-LTR survive a torn corner, sample a lens's distortion at many distances from the center, and give {fig:corners-ltr} corners for {fig:unknowns} unknowns, so the fit is far more precise than any one corner. The load-block sheet GL-CF25-LTR-D carries {fig:markers-d}.

sections.heading: Five things that would have failed silently
sections.intro: OpenCV's defaults are tuned for cameras, where a marker is a small part of the picture. GroupLab wants many corners on a flat sheet held still. None of these would have stopped a marker decoding. Each would have quietly made every measurement worse. Three are OpenCV settings and two are corrections to what OpenCV hands back, and GroupLab changes other defaults besides, such as how finely each cell of a marker is sampled.

cards.title: Corner refinement is off
cards.text: The accuracy target is a thousandth of an inch, {fig:accuracy-px} at 600 dpi. Unrefined corners would not come close. GroupLab refines every corner to a fraction of a pixel in its own code, which also gives the same corner on every platform.

cards.title: The threshold window is sized for webcams
cards.text: At 600 dpi a 4.0 mm marker is {fig:marker-px} across, far larger than the default window expects. The window is sized from the expected marker.

cards.title: OpenCV's 36h11 codes are turned 180 degrees
cards.text: Identifiers still decode, so nothing looks wrong, but the corner order is reversed. It would have shown up as a target that registers slightly badly, blamed on the printer. GroupLab prints the official orientation and turns OpenCV's corners back, tested against all {fig:tag-codes} codes.

cards.title: Results come back in any order
cards.text: The macOS runner returned markers in a different order, and RANSAC samples by position in the list, so one image could give two answers. Every detection is sorted by identifier before anything is measured.

cards.title: Shape can only be checked after decoding
cards.text: Every false marker seen on the real scans was a sliver. The size gate is given to OpenCV in advance as a minimum perimeter; the side-ratio gate cannot be, so it runs on what decoded. Both are recorded as reasons of their own.

sections.heading: Finding holes by their size, in inches
sections.intro: After the printed artwork has been subtracted, what is left is a residual image. OpenCV's morphology then cleans it by shape and size. Every radius is written in inches and converted with the scale the markers measured, so the same numbers run unchanged on a 300 dpi and a 600 dpi scan, and are meant to hold down to a 93 dpi picture from a messaging app.

items.caption: **Residual.** Observed minus expected, as a fraction of the paper-to-ink range. A hole's rim, a registration sliver along a printed ring, a speck.
**Open.** A disk of the opening radius: anything thinner disappears, the slivers and the speck.
**Threshold.** A fraction of the local range, never a gray level.
**Close and fill.** A disk of the closing radius bridges the gap in a C-shaped rim, and the inside is filled.
**Convex hull.** Its size is judged against the caliber; the center is weighted by the residual.

items.label: the threshold, a fraction of the local paper-to-ink range

cards.title: Why not a gray level
cards.text: An absolute gray threshold was measured needing {fig:gray-600} at 600 dpi, {fig:gray-300} at 300 dpi and {fig:gray-93} at 93 dpi on the same physical targets, because a rim averaged over fewer, larger pixels looks paler. A relative threshold and radii in inches need none of that tuning. How these numbers were chosen is on the hole detector's page.

sections.heading: Why four steps left OpenCV

items: The accuracy record is rerun on Windows, Linux and macOS. Linux matched to the precision reported; macOS gave different figures in two measurements. The differences were traced to four native floating-point steps: a perspective warp, sub-pixel corner refinement, the homography's final refinement, and the contour refinement, which fits lines in single precision. Turning OpenCV's optimized paths off did not help, so the cause was the native arithmetic itself.

Those four now run in GroupLab's own code using only addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and square root in a fixed order, which every processor rounds identically. The one exponential is a series; no sum is vectorized. OpenCV keeps the integer work, finding and decoding candidates and choosing RANSAC's inliers, which was already identical everywhere. Since then macOS prints the same figures as the other two.

cards.title: The four steps, in GroupLab's code
cards.text: Perspective warp · sub-pixel corner refinement · the homography's final refinement · contour refinement

sections.heading: Two detectors, because neither is enough

items: OpenCV's plain QR detector missed the codes on a 600 dpi scan, a tile and a photograph. The WeChat detector, used without its neural network models, found all three, but hands back text through UTF-8, so every byte above 0x7F in the binary frame became a replacement character and no frame passed its CRC.

So WeChat finds each code and the plain decoder reads it at those corners; its one-byte-per-character text turns back into the exact bytes. Codes are tried at several sizes, then in each corner third of the page, then in smaller corner squares, because every sheet keeps its codes near its corners; and, where that fails, each code is cut out where the markers say it is and read enlarged, two to four times.

cards.title: Where it lives
cards.text: The same source file reads the codes on the desktop, on the command line and on Android.

sections.heading: The parts that are GroupLab's own

cards.title: Drawing the target
cards.text: The sheet you print, and the expected image it is compared with.

cards.title: Fitting the paper
cards.text: The lens model by Levenberg-Marquardt, the bending surfaces and the thin-plate spline.

cards.title: Deciding what is a hole
cards.text: The size gate from the caliber, torn and partial holes, splits, flags. No learned model decides.

cards.title: Assigning shots
cards.text: Shots go to bulls by optimal one-to-one matching.

cards.title: Every statistic
cards.text: Checked key by key against the shotGroups R package on {fig:sg-datasets} reference datasets wherever it computes the same thing, and against the specification's own tables otherwise.

cards.title: The picture check
cards.text: And its score, from focus, exposure, angle, resolution, the markers read, the evenness of the light and the fit's own error.

hole-detection.pageTitle: How the hole detector was built
hole-detection.description: How GroupLab's hole detector was measured into existence: a survey of real holes, a written test, synthetic sheets, and every miss on real paper turned into a rule.
hole-detection.title: How the hole detector was built
hole-detection.lead: GroupLab's detector was not trained, and it was not guessed. It was measured into existence: {fig:survey-holes} real hole measurements first, a written test it had to pass second, synthetic sheets to practice on third, and then every miss on real paper turned into a rule with its reason written beside it.

stats.caption: hole measurements on {fig:survey-files-measured} scans of commercial targets, before GroupLab's detector was written
findings that changed the design: {fig:findings-overturned} assumptions overturned, one confirmed
a hole is wider than any printed line, on every target in the survey
learned models: every decision is a rule you can read

sections.heading: Subtract what was printed

items.caption: The photo, minus what was printed, leaves the holes.

items: A generic detector has to tell a bullet hole from a printed ring, a numeral, a barcode and a pen stroke. GroupLab printed the sheet, so it knows where every printed line is to a fraction of a millimeter. It draws that artwork again, lays it exactly over the photo through the markers, and subtracts it. Rings, numbers and bulls cancel out. What is left is everything that was not printed: the holes, and anything written on the sheet, which the definition's exclusion zones and the classifier then deal with.
This is called render-and-difference. The rest of this page is how its details were decided.

sections.heading: {fig:survey-holes} holes, and five findings that changed the design
sections.intro: Before a line of GroupLab's detector was written, {fig:survey-files} scanned files of {fig:survey-targets} commercial targets were measured by a Python and OpenCV harness: {fig:survey-holes} hole measurements on {fig:survey-files-measured} of them. Every number in the survey is labeled measured, estimated, eyeballed or not measured. The design had listed what a hole looks like. The survey checked each item.

cards.title: A hole has a bright center
text: The design said every hole shows the white scanner lid through it. Measured, the center is on average darker than paper, and a quarter of holes have a center within {fig:paper-levels} of the paper around them. No brightness cut separates holes from paper.
**Core {fig:core-darker} darker than paper · {fig:core-at-paper} at paper level**

cards.title: A hole is round
text: A bullet hole in paper is a lobed star. Any roundness test throws away real holes in proportion to how strictly it is set, which is exactly why a filled-circle detector fails.
**Rim radius varies by {fig:rim-cv} of its mean**

cards.title: The naive baseline is weak
text: Tuned for one picture, a Hough circle detector finds nearly every hole. The real problem is that its best setting changes from picture to picture, so the test had to change.
**{fig:hough-best} at one setting · {fig:hough-worst} at another**

cards.title: Color tells a hole apart
text: Chroma works on color-printed targets and does nothing on black or gray ones; brightness is the reverse. On a grayscale target the ring and the hole are the same gray. The channel must be chosen for each picture, from a measurement.
**Best separation {fig:fisher} on the grayscale target**

cards.title: Scale holds everywhere
text: Every printed feature on every target is at most {fig:printed-max} wide; every hole is {fig:hole-range} across. The gap holds on every style, including the grayscale one, and survives any resolution because it is in inches.
**Holes are {fig:scale-ratio-words} wider than any printed line**

cards.title: What that left
cards.text: Not brightness, not roundness, not color. Scale, measured in inches, is the primary test, and everything else refines it.

items.caption: **Widths on real targets, inches.** An opening with a disk wider than the widest printed line erases all printed line work while every hole survives it. That is why one opening erases the printed lines of every style in the survey, whatever the artwork. Hand ink overlaps both, so it is a job for classification, not morphology.

sections.heading: A gate that rewards stability, not luck
sections.intro: The original plan said the detector must beat a naive baseline of about {fig:baseline-plan}. The survey showed a tuned Hough circle detector finds {fig:hough-best} holes on the reference scan, but only at one setting: at an accumulator threshold of {fig:hough-t1} it finds {fig:hough-f1}, at {fig:hough-t2} it finds {fig:hough-f2}, at {fig:hough-t3} it finds none. Naive methods are not bad at finding holes. They are bad at finding them without being tuned for each picture, which is useless in an app. So the gate was rewritten.

head: Gate
Requirement
Why
rows: At least {fig:g1} of holes across all {fig:survey-files-measured} files, with one set of settings and no per-image tuning
Beats the tuned baseline while forbidding what makes it useless: tuning per picture.
At most one false mark per target, and none from the printed artwork
Rings, numerals and dots were already rejected on size; what remained was text, barcodes and handwriting.
Still above {fig:g3} when every threshold moves by {fig:g3-move} either way
The test the naive methods fail. It is what separates a shippable detector from a lucky one.
Proves no absolute gray-level threshold survived.
At least {fig:g5} on the grayscale target
The hardest file: no color at all, ring and hole the same gray. If it works there it works anywhere.

sections.heading: Holes drawn from the survey's own numbers
sections.intro: None of the {fig:survey-files} scans was a GroupLab sheet, and render-and-difference needs one. So GroupLab draws its own shot sheets: the real render of GL-CF25-LTR, with holes whose shapes come from the survey. Development used seeds {fig:seeds-dev}. Seeds {fig:seeds-held} were kept aside and run once, at the end, so the result is not the product of tuning to the test. Every synthetic score on this page is an upper bound, not a prediction for paper.

cards.title: What a synthetic hole is
cards.text: A dark rim at a set radius, lobed by four patterns of narrow outward spikes, with {fig:harmonics} lobes around the rim, so it is a ragged star, not a circle. A rim band of measured width and darkness. A core where the paper is gone, showing the scanner lid or, in the dark-backing case, a board. A disturbed zone outside the rim that recovers to paper. Holes on printed ink get the different rim the survey measured there. Over the page: hand ink, a paper gradient, a {fig:syn-blur} blur and noise.

head: How real they are
Real
Synthetic
blocks.caption: Measured by the same baseline, on {fig:real-n} real holes on bare paper. Calibration was limited to {fig:calib-rounds} rounds and the gap was published, not hidden: synthetic holes are {fig:syn-wider} wider, {fig:syn-darker} darker in the core and {fig:syn-ragged} less ragged, all of which make them easier. Every synthetic score is an upper bound.

head: Change, and why
One per bull
Two per bull
Registration off
rows: **The survey's opening, radius {fig:open-survey}.** Every miss was a thin rim around a pale center, erased by a disk wider than the rim.
**Opening cut to radius {fig:open-r}.** In a difference the artwork has already cancelled, so the opening only removes registration slivers. It broke registration tolerance instead.
**Each bull cell aligned by phase correlation.** The printed rings are fiducials too, so each cell lines itself up locally.

**Merged neighbors split; oversized holes flagged.** Single holes stretch to {fig:elong-single} at the 99th percentile ({fig:elong-worst} at worst); merged pairs from {fig:elong-pairs}. The split point sits between them.
blocks.caption: Found within {fig:found-within}, 600 dpi, development seeds; the last column with the registration off by {fig:reg-off}. Synthetic sheets, an upper bound, as first read on {fig:date-synthetic} at a split of {fig:split-first}.

head: Sheets
Render-diff
Baseline
Median error, in
blocks.caption: Found within {fig:found-within}, as first read on {fig:date-synthetic} at a split of {fig:split-first}. Median center error for render-and-difference against the baseline's. It kept every hole with the registration off by up to {fig:reg-holds}, and lost everything from {fig:reg-lost}, which says exactly how good registration must be. Re-recorded at today's split of {fig:split-now}: two per bull {fig:held-now-600} at 600 dpi and {fig:held-now-300} at 300 dpi; one per bull unchanged.

head: Case
Found
Strays
Baseline
blocks.caption: As first read at a split of {fig:split-first}. Overlapping pairs are found about half the time, by either method. Arrowheads drawn in the cells made {fig:hard-3-strays} strays at first, {fig:hard-strays-now} with today's settings, which is why position and exclusion zones matter as much as shape. At today's split overlapping pairs read {fig:hard-overlap-now}.

sections.heading: Every miss became a rule, with its reason
sections.intro: Synthetic sheets set the starting point. The developer's own range sheets then found what synthesis could not draw. The rule that came out of it: GroupLab may miss a hole, but it may never miss one silently. A missed shot is visible to the shooter who fired it; an invented one is not, so inventing is the worse mistake.

items.title: Do not cut real holes in two
items.happened: The split point between one hole and two merged holes was set at an elongation of {fig:split-first} from synthetic holes. On real paper, a hole joined to printed or photographed ink was cut in two, inventing a shot nobody could see.
items.rule: The split is at {fig:split-now}, where no real hole in the collection is split. A merged pair left whole is the louder failure: one mark about twice a hole's area, which the oversize flag reports.

items.title: A torn hole is still a hole
items.happened: Fifteen shots fired, fourteen found, and an empty review queue. The fifteenth was seen, measured at {fig:torn-size}, and refused for a solidity of {fig:torn-solidity} against a floor of {fig:solidity-floor}. Lowering the floor would have let in handwriting at {fig:handwriting-solidity}.
items.rule: A ragged mark is rescued only when it is the right size for the stated caliber, inside a bull's cell, and near the cell's middle. This is the defect that started the never-silent rule.

items.title: Holes are smaller than bullets
items.happened: Five real .22 LR holes of {fig:lr22-holes} were refused by a fixed {fig:fixed-floor} floor. Paper stretches ahead of the bullet and closes behind it; the smallest measured {fig:lr22-min} of its caliber.
items.rule: A stated caliber sets the floor at {fig:size-floor} of the caliber, a little below the worst seen so the next slightly worse hole is not refused. Without a caliber the old floor stands.

items.title: A shot that missed the bull still counts
items.happened: Two holes just off the bull grid were refused by the position rule that had removed every false mark in the survey. Dropping the rule would trade two misses for an unknown number of inventions.
items.rule: A mark within one cell width of the grid is kept, marked as outside the grid, left unassigned and shown to the shooter. Far out in the margins is still refused.

items.title: Half a hole at the edge of the picture
items.happened: A hole cut by the edge of the scan has half the area, reads as about seven tenths the width, and was refused as a speck.
items.rule: For a mark touching the edge, the diameter comes from its extent along that edge, and it is marked partial because its center rests on less evidence.

items.title: One hole or two, on photographs
items.happened: Judged against the stated caliber, one 15-shot photograph had all fifteen holes flagged as possibly two shots.
items.rule: Each mark is compared with the sheet's own other marks instead. That brought fifteen flags to one, and left scans exactly as they were.

items.title: A center from the edge, not the shadow
items.happened: A flatbed lights from one side, so a hole in card stock carries a shadow on the same side every time, and a center from the dark area is pulled toward it.
items.rule: Edges are found along rays from the center, each weighted by how sharp its crossing is, and a circle fitted to them. It measures alongside the detector's center until the comparison decides.

sections.heading: Shadows, glare, blur, curl
sections.intro: A rendered GL-CF25-LTR with one synthetic hole on each of its {fig:scoring-bulls} scoring bulls, two seeds, each degraded one way and read by the whole pipeline as a photograph. A hole counts as found within {fig:stress-within}. Synthetic holes, so an upper bound.

cards.title: Curl: 0 of 25, and fixed the same day
text: A sheet bowed by {fig:curl-px} across its width at 300 dpi, about {fig:curl-in}, read all {fig:markers-ltr} of its markers and still did not register, because a homography, even with lens terms, is flat. That was geometry, not detection, and not something learning would fix.

The fix is a thin-plate spline through every marker corner: exact at each marker, bending no more than it must between them. A corner a misread marker put far from the rest is dropped and the spline refitted. The error a person is told is each marker as predicted by a mesh fitted without it. A test now requires at least {fig:curl-test} holes found on the curled sheet.

sections.heading: Not yet, and here is the test for when
sections.intro: The failures measured so far are geometry (curl) and physics (two holes in one place), not a classifier that cannot tell a hole from a mark. A learned model also needs thousands of labeled holes across calibers, papers, lights and phones, with hundreds of the hard cases. GroupLab has about {fig:labeled-holes} distinct labeled holes, an estimate. So the plan is a scoreboard first, tuning second, and a model only if both run out.

cards.title: A scoreboard
cards.text: The degradations above, and later every target people choose to send, re-read by every build. Recall, false marks and center error by condition, so no step backward goes unseen. Fully explainable.

cards.title: Automatic tuning
cards.text: The classical settings searched against the scoreboard, keeping the rule that recall holds when every threshold moves {fig:g3-move}. The same code with other constants, each with its reason.

cards.title: A small learned classifier
cards.text: Only accepting or refining candidates; markers, codes, geometry and every measurement stay classical. Worth it when tuning cannot move a failure, most likely overlaps, and a few thousand labeled holes exist.

sections.heading: What is met, and what is not

cards.title: Real commercial scan
cards.text: {fig:real-scan} hand-verified holes with no false marks on the reference scan, by the detector GroupLab's own grew from.

cards.title: Registration on paper
cards.text: Ten of ten printed sheets inside the {fig:reg-gate} gate, worst bull {fig:worst-bull}.

cards.title: Synthetic gate
cards.text: {fig:syn-gate} of holes with no false marks: one hole per bull is found completely with no strays, two per bull reaches {fig:syn-two-now} at today's split. Synthetic, so an upper bound.

cards.title: Photographs
cards.text: Flat photographs nearly pass the {fig:reg-gate} gate; mounted ones do not yet, and wait on photographs of mounted GroupLab sheets.

cards.title: Overlapping holes
cards.text: The largest real failure. On {fig:tight-photos} photographs of a commercial grid target shot in tight five-shot groups, the detector built from the scans, for sheets GroupLab did not print, found {fig:tight-found} shots as marks of their own.

pipeline.pageTitle: Follow one target, stage by stage
pipeline.description: One target followed from printing to the report through every stage of GroupLab's pipeline, with a real run's record at the end.
pipeline.title: Follow one target, stage by stage
pipeline.lead: Eight steps a shooter would name, {fig:stages} stages in the pipeline's specification. Each stage has a defined input and output, a way to fail, and a record of what it decided and what it threw away, so every number can be traced back to the pixels it came from.

stats.caption: shots found and assigned in the real run at the foot of this page

sections.heading: Print
sections.intro: The sheet is born from a GLTD definition, and everything GroupLab will later need to read it is printed on it.

items.caption: Step 1: print.

items.label: markers on GL-CF25-LTR, on the corners of its cell lattice
per marker with its quiet zone

cards.title: The definition
text: Bulls, rings, markers and QR codes, all in page units.
Exclusion zones that can never hold a shot: the data block a shooter writes a load in, the codes with their quiet zones, the marker footprints and the identifier text.

cards.title: The render
text: AprilTag 36h11 markers of {fig:marker-module} squares, {fig:marker-size} across, where the cell lines cross and nothing else is in the way; {fig:markers-tile} on a 300 yard tile.
A GLTD-B frame in every QR code: the whole definition, a CRC-32 over it and a tile index; the sheet's identifier is computed from the definition.
Markers in the family's official orientation, whatever OpenCV's dictionary holds.

sections.heading: Shoot
sections.intro: Nothing runs, but the physics decides what GroupLab will see. Paper stretches ahead of the bullet and closes behind it, so the hole is narrower than the bullet, by a roughly constant amount rather than a proportion.

items.caption: Step 2: shoot.

cards.title: What holes measure
text: About {fig:allowance} narrower than the bullet, with a spread of {fig:allowance-sd}: modeled as a fixed allowance, not a scale factor.
.338 holes measured {fig:ratio-338} of caliber; a .22 LR hole as little as {fig:lr22-min}.

On printed ink a hole's rim is shallower and less even (its darkest point V {fig:ink-rim} against {fig:paper-rim} on paper), its dark band about {fig:ink-band} thicker, and it measures about {fig:ink-width} smaller; the inside of the hole is unchanged.

sections.heading: Capture
sections.intro: A scan or a photograph becomes one image with a record of where it came from, and the sheet names its own definition.

items.caption: Step 3: capture.

items.label: live analysis stream on the phone

cards.title: Decode
text: The file is decoded as the camera or scanner stored it. PNG and JPEG are read.
The EXIF orientation is recorded, not applied, because the markers do not care which way up the sheet is.

cards.title: Identify
text: QR codes tried at full, double, half and quarter size, stopping at the first size that gives a GLTD-B frame passing its CRC; a size that would exceed {fig:identify-cap} is skipped.
When no size gives a code, each code is cut out where the markers put it and read enlarged {fig:crop-scales} times.
Codes naming two definitions, or one not available, are refused with the reason. Nothing is guessed from the markers, which the built-in sheets share.
{fig:identify-named} Phase 0 images named, on Windows, Linux and macOS alike, and none named wrongly.

cards.title: The camera
text: One instruction at a time, in order: move back, move closer, less angle, hold steadier, more or less light.
Guided mode fires after {fig:ready-frames} ready frames in a row; every picture is then checked and scored.

sections.heading: Register
sections.intro: The markers turn pixels into page coordinates. This is where a photo's angle, a lens's bulge and a curled sheet are taken out.

items.caption: Step 4: register.

items.label: of {fig:mat-holes} holes found once detection was kept inside the sheet

cards.title: Scale
text: In order of authority: the markers, then the file's DPI tag, then the content, then the person.
The tag was accurate to better than {fig:tag-accuracy} on all {fig:tagged-files} files that carry one; a messaging-app picture with no tag was derived twice, at {fig:derived-dpi}.
A provisional scale seeds the marker search, and is replaced once markers are found.

cards.title: Markers
text: Sub-pixel corners, refined in GroupLab's own code; threshold window sized for the marker; area and side-ratio gates as separate reasons.
If markers are lost: any four or more still register the sheet, fitted with RANSAC; with fewer, GroupLab stops and says how many it found.

cards.title: Register
text: Scans: a homography. On a crumpled, taped sheet it left {fig:rms-homography} rms, where a similarity left {fig:rms-similarity}, and a more complex surface gained only {fig:rms-gain}.
Never less than affine: scanners shear rows against columns by {fig:scanner-shear}.
Photographs: a homography with two radial lens terms, fitted by Levenberg-Marquardt from the markers alone, with no camera data.
Bent paper: a thin-plate spline through every corner, and developable surfaces kept only when an F test says the bend is real.

cards.title: Verify
text: Print scale reported on each axis, not silently corrected.

From here on only pixels inside the registered sheet can become a candidate: on one photo the dark mat around the sheet merged into a blob a foot across, and 0 of {fig:mat-holes} holes were found until it was masked.

sections.heading: Detect
sections.intro: Render the sheet as printed, lay it over the photo, subtract, and judge what is left.

items.caption: Step 5: detect.

items.label: threshold, a fraction of paper-to-ink range

cards.title: Render
text: The definition rasterized and resampled through the registration, on a grid and interpolated between.
Paper: the {fig:paper-pct} percentile of paper pixels in {fig:paper-block-words} blocks, smoothed. Ink: the median ratio of observed to paper where the render calls ink.
Each bull cell aligned by phase correlation, up to {fig:cell-shift}; the rest of the page by the median of those shifts. Exclusion zones masked hard.

cards.title: Difference
text: The absolute difference of observed and expected, both normalized by paper, as a fraction of the paper-to-ink range.
Counted in both directions, because a hole in a solid black bull makes the page lighter, not darker.

cards.title: Candidates
text: Open with a disk of radius {fig:open-r}, threshold at {fig:threshold}, close with a disk of radius {fig:close-r}, fill, take each blob's convex hull.
Every radius in inches, converted with the scale S1 settled.

cards.title: Classify
text: Size against the stated caliber, floor {fig:size-floor} of it; solidity and aspect, with the torn-hole rescue.
Position: outside every cell is refused, except within one cell width of the grid, kept and marked.

Elongation of {fig:split-now} or more is split into two holes, both flagged; a mark with the area of {fig:oversize} single holes or more is flagged as oversized, a single hole being the caliber's or the sheet's own typical mark.
Center: weighted by the residual, over the whole disturbed area, not a fitted circle.

sections.heading: Assign
sections.intro: Nearest bull is not the rule. The rule is the matching of shots to bulls, one each, that minimizes the total distance, because one shot per bull is what the sheet was designed around.

items.caption: Step 6: assign.

items.label: shots per surveyed target outside their own cell
shot nearest bull got wrong in the survey; matching gets it right

cards.title: Three cases
text: As many shots as bulls, or fewer: optimal one-to-one matching.
More shots than bulls: never forced, because forcing manufactures confident wrong answers. Nearest bull within a distance, every shot flagged, and the person told the counts disagree.
A margin under {fig:assign-margin} between the best and second-best bull is flagged either way.

cards.title: The case that proves it
text: On one commercial scan, a hole {fig:case-4} from bull 4 and {fig:case-9} from bull 9. Nearest bull gives it to 4, which already has a shot {fig:case-other} away; bull 9 has none. Matching gets it right.

sections.heading: Combine
sections.intro: Sheets of one load, or the tiles of one large target, become one group. Only bookkeeping, never geometry, joins them.

items.caption: Step 7: combine.

items.label: effect of tile alignment on the group

cards.title: Pool
text: Each tile runs S0 to S9 on its own and every shot is an offset from its own bull, so tape gaps and sheets stapled out of square add nothing.
The tile index in each frame maps local bulls to the assembly. Every tile present once; a missing tile is reported as missing bulls, not dropped.
A sheet read twice counts once, and GroupLab says so.
A contested assignment on one tile stays contested in the composite.

sections.heading: Report
sections.intro: The figures, each with a range for how sure it is, from a statistics library compared with R's shotGroups on every build.

items.caption: Step 8: report.

cards.title: What is reported
text: Mean radius, estimated as sigma times the square root of pi over two; CEP 50 and 90; extreme spread; each with its interval.
A shot left out is out of every figure, and shown as left out.
The offsets for a zero from the statistics, and the drop, wind and hit chance at distance from the ballistics.

sections.heading: Every stage writes down what it did
sections.intro: Each stage writes a record: the settings it actually used (in inches and in the pixels they became), the decisions it made with the alternatives it turned down, and every candidate it rejected with the reason. The rejections are the interesting half: they turn "no shot here" into "a mark 0.058 in across, under the 0.150 in floor". Below is a real run of grouplab analyze on a sample in the repository, a 600 dpi scan of GL-CF25-LTR-D with {fig:sample-shots} shots. In code, S5 to S8 are recorded as one stage and S10 is called group.

                            candidates: 44 definitions
